## Where we've been

```{r}
#| label: power-setup
#| include: false

# Power and the Type S / Type M errors are one scene built up over several
# slides (power-anim/power.js): each slide embeds the script with the stage it
# opens on and the stage its last fragment reaches. The effect sizes are in
# standard errors, delta = (mu - mu0) / SE(Ybar); 2.8 gives the conventional
# 80% power and 0.25 an underpowered design like those in Gelman and Carlin
power_data <- jsonlite::toJSON(list(alpha = 0.05, deltas = c(1, 2, 2.8, 4),
                                    low = 0.25),
                               auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = NA)
power_anim <- function(from, to) {
  cat("```{=html}",
      '<div class="pw-anim"></div>',
      "<script>",
      "(", readLines("power-anim/power.js"), ")(document.currentScript.previousElementSibling,",
      power_data, ", { from: ", from, ", to: ", to, " });",
      "</script>",
      rep('<span class="fragment pw-step"></span>', to - from),
      "```", sep = "\n")
}
```

## Where we've been

```{r}
#| label: cef-setup
#| include: false

# A sample of 150 from a population whose CEF is linear,
# E[Y | X] = 2 + 0.6 X with N(0, 1.2^2) errors and X ~ N(5, 1.6^2), so the
# mean of Y is mu = 2 + 0.6 * 5 = 5. The horizontal line at mu pivots about
# (E[X], E[Y]) into the CEF (cef-anim/cef.js): each slide embeds the script
# with the stage it opens on and the stage its last fragment reaches
set.seed(812)
cef_pop <- list(b0 = 2, b1 = 0.6, sigma = 1.2, mux = 5, sdx = 1.6)
cef_x <- rnorm(150, cef_pop$mux, cef_pop$sdx)
cef_y <- cef_pop$b0 + cef_pop$b1 * cef_x + rnorm(150, 0, cef_pop$sigma)
keep <- cef_x > 0 & cef_x < 10 & cef_y > 0 & cef_y < 10
cef_data <- jsonlite::toJSON(c(cef_pop,
                               list(x = round(cef_x[keep], 3), y = round(cef_y[keep], 3),
                                    xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(0, 10))),
                             auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = NA)
cef_anim <- function(from, to) {
  cat("```{=html}",
      '<div class="cf-anim"></div>',
      "<script>",
      "(", readLines("cef-anim/cef.js"), ")(document.currentScript.previousElementSibling,",
      cef_data, ", { from: ", from, ", to: ", to, " });",
      "</script>",
      rep('<span class="fragment cf-step"></span>', to - from),
      "```", sep = "\n")
}
```

## Regression

:::{.incremental}

- In the social sciences, we often want to understand how our **prediction** for an outcome variable $Y_i$ changes depending on the values of some set of covariates $\mathbf{X}_i$
  - **Description**: A parsimonious summary of the data
  - **Forecasting**: Given a *new* value of $\mathbf{X}_i$, what's our best prediction for $Y_i$?
  - **Adjustment for causal inference**: Can we **explain away** $Y_i$ with confounders $\mathbf{X}_i$ to make our causal assumptions more credible?

- In all cases, our **estimand** changes from a single parameter to a **function** 
  - The **conditional expectation function**

  $$\mu(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid \mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}]$$
:::

## Running Example: Hostile sexism and support for Trump

::: {.incremental}

- Do **gender attitudes** predict support for right-wing political candidates even after we adjust for partisanship?
  - One particular attitude measured by political psychologists is **hostile sexism**
    - Antagonism towards women seen as seeking power or challenging traditional gender roles [@glick1996ambivalent]
  - In 2016, hostile sexism predicted support for Trump over Clinton even after adjusting for partisanship and other predictors [@winter2023hostile]. 
    - Additionally, it appears to contribute to the **education gap** in political attitudes among white voters [@schaffner2018understanding]
  - Does the relationship hold up in 2024?

- **Outcome** $Y_i$: Trump feeling thermometer (0-100) from the 2024 ANES [@anes2024timeseries]

- **Regressor** $X_i$: responses to four statements, each on a 5-point scale, rescaled to $[0, 1]$ and averaged

  ::: {style="font-size: 0.72em"}
  1) "Many women interpret innocent remarks or acts as being sexist." (agree-disagree)
  2) "Women seek to gain power by getting control over men." (agree-disagree)
  3) "When women demand equality these days, how often are they actually seeking special favors?" (always-never)
  4) "When women complain about discrimination, how often do they cause more problems than they solve?" (always-never)
  :::

:::

## Marginal distributions

```{r}
#| label: anes-load
#| include: false
#| message: false

library(tidyverse)
# 2024 ANES: the Trump thermometer and the four-item hostile sexism scale
# (data/prepare_data.R builds the extract from the full release)
anes <- read_csv("data/anes24_sexism.csv") |>
  filter(!is.na(ft_trump), !is.na(hostile_sexism))
```

```{r}
#| label: reg-setup
#| include: false

theme_reg <- theme_minimal(base_size = 18) +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(),
        axis.line = element_line(colour = "#333333"),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
        plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#F7F7F7", colour = NA))

# X takes 17 values and the thermometer heaps at multiples of 5, so many
# respondents share a point: a low alpha lets the stacks show as darker dots
base_plot <- function(alpha = 0.06) {
  ggplot() +
    geom_point(data = anes, aes(hostile_sexism, ft_trump), colour = "#333333", alpha = alpha,
               size = 3, stroke = 0) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.25)) +
    scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 100, 25)) +
    labs(x = "Hostile sexism", y = "Trump thermometer") +
    theme_reg
}
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 5.8
#| fig-align: center

# One panel per variable, each on its own x range, with solid lines at the
# means. The thermometer heaps at 0, 15, 30, ..., 85, 100, so its bins are
# [0, 10), ..., [90, 100] as in week 8; hostile sexism gets one bar per value
marg <- anes |>
  select(ft_trump, hostile_sexism) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "var", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(var = factor(var, levels = c("ft_trump", "hostile_sexism"),
                      labels = c("Trump thermometer (Y)", "Hostile sexism (X)")))
marg_means <- marg |> summarize(value = mean(value), .by = var)

ggplot(marg, aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(data = \(d) filter(d, var == "Trump thermometer (Y)"), breaks = seq(0, 100, 10),
                 closed = "left", fill = "#0479a8", colour = "#F7F7F7") +
  geom_histogram(data = \(d) filter(d, var == "Hostile sexism (X)"), binwidth = 1 / 16, center = 0,
                 fill = "#0479a8", colour = "#F7F7F7") +
  geom_vline(data = marg_means, aes(xintercept = value), linewidth = 1.4, colour = "#333333") +
  facet_wrap(~ var, nrow = 1, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Number of respondents") +
  theme_reg +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 20), panel.spacing.x = unit(2, "lines"))

## Why models?

::: {.incremental}

- It might seem like we can just use the same **sample mean** estimator as before but on **subsets of the data**
  - With discrete covariates, **we can!**
  - Regression is just taking a **conditional** mean.

- Suppose we separated our respondents into two "bins": high sexism and low sexism
  - Call respondents who agree with the statements on average ($X_i > 0.5$) **high** and those below **low**
  - The CEF is just **two** distinct quantities.
  - We can estimate each by a **sample mean** within its group

    $$\hat{\mu}(\text{high}) = \frac{1}{n_{\text{high}}}\sum_{i : X_i > 0.5} Y_i \qquad \widehat{SE}\left(\hat{\mu}(\text{high})\right) = \frac{\hat{\sigma}_{\text{high}}}{\sqrt{n_{\text{high}}}}$$

  - Everything from the last three weeks carries through.
    - Under i.i.d. sampling from the target population, it's unbiased, consistent, asymptotically normal

:::

## Two groups

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 5.6
#| fig-align: center

two_groups <- anes |>
  mutate(group = if_else(hostile_sexism > 0.5, "high", "low")) |>
  summarize(n = n(), mean = mean(ft_trump), se = sd(ft_trump) / sqrt(n),
            .by = group) |>
  mutate(lower = mean - qnorm(0.975) * se, upper = mean + qnorm(0.975) * se)

# Each group's mean as a step across its range of X, with its 95% CI shaded
# and labeled. The step changes halfway between 0.5 and the next value, 0.5625
cut_x <- 0.53125
steps <- two_groups |>
  mutate(xmin = if_else(group == "low", -0.02, cut_x),
         xmax = if_else(group == "low", cut_x, 1.02),
         label = sprintf("%s: %.1f  [%.1f, %.1f]\nn = %s", if_else(group == "low", "Low", "High"),
                         mean, lower, upper, format(n, big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE)))
base_plot() +
  geom_rect(data = steps, aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = lower, ymax = upper),
            fill = "#0479a8", alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_segment(data = steps, aes(x = xmin, xend = xmax, y = mean, yend = mean),
               colour = "#0479a8", linewidth = 1.6) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = cut_x, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#333333") +
  geom_label(data = steps, aes((xmin + xmax) / 2, mean + 12, label = label),
             size = 5.5, colour = "#0479a8", fill = "#F7F7F7", label.size = 0, lineheight = 0.9)
```

::: {.incremental}

- High-sexism respondents rate Trump `r with(two_groups, sprintf("%.1f", mean[group == "high"] - mean[group == "low"]))` points more warmly.

:::

## Binning on every value of $X$

::: {.incremental}

- Our hostile sexism measure only has **17** distinct values. We can calculate a conditional mean at **every** one
  $$\hat{\mu}(x) = \frac{1}{n_x}\sum_{i : X_i = x} Y_i \qquad n_x = \sum_{i=1}^n I(X_i = x)$$

- **No assumptions** about the shape of $\mu(x)$. Our estimator is fully **nonparametric**

- But the precision at each $x$ depends **only** on $n_x$: $\widehat{SE}\left(\hat{\mu}(x)\right) = \hat{\sigma}_x / \sqrt{n_x}$
  - Some bins are very small!

:::

## Binning on every value of $X$

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 5.6
#| fig-align: center

bins <- anes |>
  summarize(n = n(), mean = mean(ft_trump), se = sd(ft_trump) / sqrt(n),
            .by = hostile_sexism) |>
  mutate(t_crit = qt(0.975, df = n - 1),   # small bins: t, not normal
         lower = mean - t_crit * se,
         upper = mean + t_crit * se) |>
  arrange(hostile_sexism)

# The 17 conditional means with t intervals, and each bin's size along the
# bottom. The y range is held at the thermometer's, so the two sparsest
# bins' intervals run off the plot
base_plot() +
  geom_pointrange(data = bins, aes(hostile_sexism, mean, ymin = lower, ymax = upper),
                  colour = "#0479a8", linewidth = 1.1, size = 0.7) +
  geom_text(data = bins, aes(hostile_sexism, -8, label = n), size = 4.2, colour = "#646569") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-9, 103))
```

::: {.incremental}

- Support rises until about $0.6$ and then appears to **level off**
- We pay for flexibility with **variance**: the top two bins only hold `r bins$n[16]` and `r bins$n[17]` respondents!

:::

## The curse of dimensionality

::: {.incremental}

- Binning worked because $X_i$ is **one** variable with **17** values, and we have thousands of respondents

- What if we want the CEF given hostile sexism **and** gender, education, race, partisanship, ideology and age?
  $$\mu(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid \mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}] \qquad \mathbf{X}_i = (X_{i1}, X_{i2}, \dotsc, X_{ik})$$

  - Binning needs a separate mean for **every combination** of covariate values
  - And if we have a **continuous** covariate, nearly *every* respondent has a unique value of that covariate

- This is the **curse of dimensionality**
  - As the number of covariates grows, the covariate **space** grows exponentially

:::

## The curse of dimensionality

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis

# Exact-match bins as covariates are added one at a time, among respondents
# with every covariate observed. "Alone" means the respondent is the only one
# in their bin; bin sizes are averaged over respondents, not bins
cc <- anes |> drop_na(gender, college, race, pid7, ideo7, age)
covs <- c(hostile_sexism = "Hostile sexism", gender = "+ gender", college = "+ college degree",
          race = "+ race", pid7 = "+ party ID (7 pt.)", ideo7 = "+ ideology (7 pt.)",
          age = "+ age")
curse <- map_dfr(seq_along(covs), \(j) {
  v <- names(covs)[1:j]
  k <- cc |> add_count(across(all_of(v)), name = "k") |> pull(k)
  tibble(label = covs[j],
         nbins = prod(map_int(v, \(x) n_distinct(cc[[x]]))),
         nonempty = nrow(distinct(cc, across(all_of(v)))),
         median_k = median(k),
         alone = mean(k == 1),
         under10 = mean(k < 10))
})
fmt <- function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE)
pct <- function(x) sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * x)
cat('```{=html}',
    "<style>",
    ".reveal .curse-table table { border-collapse: collapse; margin: 0 auto; font-size: 0.72em; border-top: 2px solid #333; border-bottom: 2px solid #333; }",
    ".reveal .curse-table table th, .reveal .curse-table table td { border: none; padding: 0.18em 0.7em; text-align: right; white-space: nowrap; }",
    ".reveal .curse-table table td:first-child, .reveal .curse-table table th:first-child { text-align: left; }",
    ".reveal .curse-table table th { font-weight: 400; color: #646569; border-bottom: 1px solid #333; }",
    "</style>",
    '<div class="curse-table"><table>',
    "<thead><tr><th>Conditioning on</th><th>Possible bins</th><th>Non-empty bins</th>",
    "<th>Median bin size</th><th>Alone in bin</th><th>In a bin of &lt; 10</th></tr></thead>",
    "<tbody>",
    paste0("<tr><td>", curse$label, "</td><td>", fmt(curse$nbins), "</td><td>", fmt(curse$nonempty),
           "</td><td>", fmt(curse$median_k), "</td><td>", pct(curse$alone), "</td><td>",
           pct(curse$under10), "</td></tr>"),
    "</tbody></table></div>",
    "```", sep = "\n")
```

::: {.incremental}

- `r fmt(nrow(cc))` respondents with every covariate observed. Once we condition on party ID and ideology, the typical respondent shares their covariate bin with only `r curse$median_k[6] - 1` others
- Add age, and `r pct(curse$alone[7])` of respondents have *unique* covariate profiles.

:::

## Borrowing strength

::: {.incremental}

- To estimate $\mu(\mathbf{x})$ where we have little data, we have to use observations at **other** values of $\mathbf{X}_i$

- That requires **assumptions** about how $\mu(\cdot)$ behaves between the points we observe. 
- For example:
  - **Smoothness**: $\mu(\cdot)$ doesn't change much between nearby $\mathbf{x}$
  - **Functional form**: $\mu(\cdot)$ has a particular shape everywhere (e.g. a line)

- This is why we need **models**. More covariates, more need to impose structure **ex-ante**

- Some alternative estimation strategies:
  - **Kernel estimators**: Average the observations *near* $\mathbf{x}$ when estimating $\mu(\mathbf{x})$
  - **Linear regression**: Assume a shape for $\mu(\cdot)$ and use **all** of the data to estimate the function.

:::

## Local averaging

::: {.incremental}

- Instead of averaging only the exact matches, average every observation within a **window** $h/2$ of $x$
  $$\hat{\mu}(x) = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n I\left(|X_i - x| \le \tfrac{h}{2}\right) Y_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n I\left(|X_i - x| \le \tfrac{h}{2}\right)}$$

- This is the same idea as our **kernel density** estimator but applied to **regression**
  - Calculate the mean at each $x$ using a window centered on $x$

- The width $h$ is a **tuning parameter**
  - Too small: few observations in each window $\leadsto$ **noisy** estimator
  - Too large: we average over a region where $\mu(x)$ changes $\leadsto$ **bias**

- Here, we're assuming a **uniform** kernel
  - But as before, we can instead let the weight on each observation **fall** with its distance from $x$

:::

## Nadaraya-Watson kernel regression

::: {.incremental}

- The **Nadaraya-Watson** estimator [@nadaraya1964estimating; @watson1964smooth]
  $$\hat{\mu}_h(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n K_h(\mathbf{X}_i - \mathbf{x})\, Y_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n K_h(\mathbf{X}_i - \mathbf{x})} = \sum_{i=1}^n w_i(\mathbf{x})\, Y_i \qquad w_i(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{K_h(\mathbf{X}_i - \mathbf{x})}{\sum_{j=1}^n K_h(\mathbf{X}_j - \mathbf{x})}$$

- A **weighted average** of the outcomes: the weights are non-negative, sum to $1$, and are larger for the observations closer to $\mathbf{x}$

- The same kernels as in density estimation, $K_h(\mathbf{u}) = K(\mathbf{u}/h)$
  - With $k$ dimensions, often use the **product kernel**: $K(\mathbf{u}) = \prod_{j=1}^k K(u_j)$ (with covariates on a common scale)
    -  The product of covariate-specific kernels (which can be uniform/triangular/etc...) 
  - Another approach is the **"nearest neighbors"** method: at each $x$, average the outcomes of the $m$ closest observations (based on some distance metric)
    - Larger windows in *sparser* parts of the covariate space.

:::

## The kernel weights

```{r}
#| label: nw-setup
#| include: false

# The Gaussian-kernel bandwidth used in the figures, the same as in the R
# example (leave-one-out cross-validation picks about 0.048)
h_nw <- 0.05
nw_at <- function(x0, h) {
  w <- dnorm((anes$hostile_sexism - x0) / h)
  sum(w * anes$ft_trump) / sum(w)
}
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 5.6
#| fig-align: center

# Gaussian weights around three target points at the chosen
# bandwidth: each point's shade is its weight, the shaded bump along the
# bottom is the kernel, and the large dot is the weighted mean. Many
# respondents share each (x, y), and stacked transparent points would go dark
# whatever their weight, so each distinct point is drawn once (faint grey
# for where the data are, then ink shaded by its weight relative to K(0))
x0s <- c(0.125, 0.5, 0.875)
panel_lab <- sprintf("x = %s", x0s)
pts <- distinct(anes, hostile_sexism, ft_trump)
wts <- map_dfr(seq_along(x0s), \(j) {
  pts |>
    mutate(panel = factor(panel_lab[j], panel_lab),
           w = dnorm((hostile_sexism - x0s[j]) / h_nw) / dnorm(0))
})
bumps <- map_dfr(seq_along(x0s), \(j) {
  tibble(panel = factor(panel_lab[j], panel_lab), x = seq(0, 1, 0.002),
         k = 30 * dnorm((x - x0s[j]) / h_nw) / dnorm(0))
})
est <- tibble(panel = factor(panel_lab, panel_lab), x = x0s,
              fit = map_dbl(x0s, nw_at, h = h_nw))
ggplot() +
  geom_area(data = bumps, aes(x, k), fill = "#0479a8", alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_point(data = pts, aes(hostile_sexism, ft_trump), colour = "#9a9a9a", alpha = 0.2,
             size = 3, stroke = 0) +
  geom_point(data = wts, aes(hostile_sexism, ft_trump, alpha = 0.9 * w), colour = "#333333",
             size = 3, stroke = 0) +
  geom_vline(data = est, aes(xintercept = x), linetype = "dashed", colour = "#0479a8") +
  geom_point(data = est, aes(x, fit), colour = "#0479a8", size = 6) +
  geom_label(data = est, aes(x, fit, label = sprintf("%.1f", fit)), nudge_y = 9,
             size = 5.5, colour = "#0479a8", fill = "#F7F7F7", label.size = 0) +
  scale_alpha_identity() +
  facet_wrap(~ panel) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.5)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 100, 25)) +
  labs(x = "Hostile sexism", y = "Trump thermometer") +
  theme_reg
```

::: {.incremental}

- Gaussian kernel, $h = `r sprintf("%.2f", h_nw)`$

:::

## Nadaraya-Watson in R

```{r}
# Nadaraya-Watson with a Gaussian kernel: a weighted mean of Y around x0
nw <- function(x0, x, y, h) {
  w <- dnorm((x - x0) / h)
  sum(w * y) / sum(w)
}

grid <- (0:100) / 100
nw_fit <- tibble(hostile_sexism = grid,
                 fit = map_dbl(grid, nw, x = anes$hostile_sexism,
                               y = anes$ft_trump, h = 0.05))
nw_fit |> filter(hostile_sexism %in% c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1))
```

## Choosing the bandwidth

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 5.6
#| fig-align: center

# Nadaraya-Watson fits at a too-small bandwidth (which reproduces the bins),
# the one used throughout and a too-large one, over the 17 bin means
hs <- c(0.01, h_nw, 0.3)
hs_lab <- c("h = 0.01: too small", sprintf("h = %.2f", h_nw), "h = 0.3: too large")
fits <- map_dfr(seq_along(hs), \(j) {
  tibble(panel = factor(hs_lab[j], hs_lab), x = (0:200) / 200,
         fit = map_dbl(x, nw_at, h = hs[j]))
})
base_plot(alpha = 0.04) +
  geom_point(data = bins, aes(hostile_sexism, mean), colour = "#333333", size = 2) +
  geom_line(data = fits, aes(x, fit), colour = "#0479a8", linewidth = 1.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.5))
```

::: {.incremental}

- The bias depends on how much $\mu(\cdot)$ **curves** and whether $\mathbf{X}_i$ are *lopsided* around $\mathbf{x}$
- The variance depends on $\Var(Y_i \mid \mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x})$ and on how many observations are around $\mathbf{x}$

:::

## From a local to a global estimator

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 5.6
#| fig-align: center

# The Nadaraya-Watson fit against the least squares line
ols <- coef(lm(ft_trump ~ hostile_sexism, data = anes))
nw_fit_h <- tibble(x = (0:200) / 200) |> mutate(fit = map_dbl(x, nw_at, h = h_nw))
base_plot(alpha = 0.04) +
  geom_line(data = nw_fit_h, aes(x, fit), colour = "#0479a8", linewidth = 1.6) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 0, xend = 1, y = ols[1], yend = ols[1] + ols[2]),
               colour = "#c5050c", linewidth = 1.6) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.97, y = 61, label = "Nadaraya-Watson", colour = "#0479a8",
           size = 6, hjust = 1) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.97, y = 105, label = "Least squares line", colour = "#c5050c",
           size = 6, hjust = 1) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 106))
```

::: {.incremental}

- What if we **assume** the CEF is a line, $\mu(x) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x$? 
  - Regardless of how many values $X_i$ takes, we're only ever estimating **two** things
- Every observation informs the fit at **every** $x$, so the line is more **precise**
  - But at the cost of bias. Where $\mu(\cdot)$ bends, the line is **biased** for the true CEF

:::

## Linear regression and ordinary least squares

## Best Linear Predictor

::: {.incremental}

- Let's restrict our focus to functions of $X$ that are **linear predictors** 
  - That is, they're **linear** combinations of the covariates and some set of **parameters**
- With a single covariate

  $$m(x) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x$$

- With **many covariates**, we write

  $$m(\mathbf{x}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \dotsc + \beta_{k-1} x_{k-1} = \mathbf{x}^\prime\boldsymbol{\beta}$$

    $$\mathbf{x} = (1, x_1, \dotsc, x_{k-1})^\prime \qquad \boldsymbol{\beta} = (\beta_0, \beta_1, \dotsc, \beta_{k-1})^\prime$$

- **Review**: Inner products

    $$\underbrace{\mathbf{x}^\prime}_{1 \times k} \quad \underbrace{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{k \times 1} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & x_1 & x_2 & \cdots & x_{k-1} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \beta_0 \\ \beta_1 \\ \beta_2 \\ \vdots \\ \beta_{k-1} \end{pmatrix} = 1 \cdot \beta_0 + x_1 \beta_1 + x_2 \beta_2 + \dotsc + x_{k-1} \beta_{k-1}$$
:::

## Best Linear Predictor

::: {.incremental}

- The **best linear predictor** is the linear predictor that **minimizes** the expected squared prediction error

  $$\boldsymbol{\beta} = \arg\min_{\mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^k} \ \mathbb{E}\big[(Y_i - \mathbf{X}_i^\prime\mathbf{b})^2\big]$$

- We found a **closed form solution** for the two-parameter case in a previous lecture

  $$\beta_1 = \frac{\Cov(X_i, Y_i)}{\Var(X_i)} \qquad \beta_0 = \mathbb{E}[Y_i] - \beta_1\,\mathbb{E}[X_i]$$

- Let's derive the **general form** for *many* covariates

:::


## Best Linear Predictor

::: {.incremental}

- We'll start by taking the **partial derivatives** of the squared errors inside the expectation with respect to the **parameters**

  $$
  \begin{aligned}
  \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathbf{b}} (Y_i - \mathbf{X}_i^\prime\mathbf{b})^2 &= \begin{pmatrix} \frac{\partial}{\partial b_0} (Y_i - \mathbf{X}_i^\prime\mathbf{b})^2 \\ \vdots \\ \frac{\partial}{\partial b_{k-1}} (Y_i - \mathbf{X}_i^\prime\mathbf{b})^2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} -2 \cdot 1 \cdot (Y_i - \mathbf{X}_i^\prime\mathbf{b}) \\ \vdots \\ -2 X_{i,k-1} (Y_i - \mathbf{X}_i^\prime\mathbf{b}) \end{pmatrix} \\[0.4em]
  &= -2\,\mathbf{X}_i (Y_i - \mathbf{X}_i^\prime\mathbf{b}) = -2\,(\mathbf{X}_i Y_i - \mathbf{X}_i\mathbf{X}_i^\prime\mathbf{b})
  \end{aligned}
  $$

- Review: outer products

  $$\underbrace{\mathbf{X}_i}_{k \times 1} \quad \underbrace{\mathbf{X}_i^\prime}_{1 \times k} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ X_{i1} \\ \vdots \\ X_{i,k-1} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & X_{i1} & \cdots & X_{i,k-1} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & X_{i1} & \cdots & X_{i,k-1} \\ X_{i1} & X_{i1}^2 & \cdots & X_{i1} X_{i,k-1} \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ X_{i,k-1} & X_{i,k-1} X_{i1} & \cdots & X_{i,k-1}^2 \end{pmatrix}$$

:::

## Best Linear Predictor

::: {.incremental}

- Take the **expected value** and set it equal to $\mathbf{0}$ to solve for $\boldsymbol{\beta}$

  $$
  \begin{aligned}
  \mathbb{E}\big[{-2}\,(\mathbf{X}_i Y_i - \mathbf{X}_i\mathbf{X}_i^\prime\boldsymbol{\beta})\big] &= \mathbf{0} \\
  \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{X}_i Y_i] - \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{X}_i\mathbf{X}_i^\prime]\,\boldsymbol{\beta} &= \mathbf{0} \\
  \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{X}_i\mathbf{X}_i^\prime]\,\boldsymbol{\beta} &= \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{X}_i Y_i] \\
  \boldsymbol{\beta} &= \big(\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{X}_i\mathbf{X}_i^\prime]\big)^{-1}\,\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{X}_i Y_i]
  \end{aligned}
  $$

- What have we **assumed**? 
- Essentially just **regularity conditions** that ensure the BLP **exists**
  - Finite mean/variance for $Y$
  - Finite means/variances/covariances for $\mathbf{X}$
  - $(\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{X}_i\mathbf{X}_i^\prime])^{-1}$ exists (no **perfect** linear dependence between covariates)

:::

## Projection error

::: {.incremental}

- What are the properties of the **error** between the true $Y_i$ and the **best linear predictor**?

  $$e_i = Y_i - m(\mathbf{X}_i) = Y_i - \mathbf{X}_i^\prime\boldsymbol{\beta}$$

- One very important property is that the projection errors are **uncorrelated** with the covariates

  $$
  \begin{aligned}
  \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{X}_i e_i] &= \mathbb{E}\big[\mathbf{X}_i (Y_i - \mathbf{X}_i^\prime\boldsymbol{\beta})\big] \\
  &= \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{X}_i Y_i] - \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{X}_i\mathbf{X}_i^\prime]\,\boldsymbol{\beta} \\
  &= \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{X}_i Y_i] - \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{X}_i\mathbf{X}_i^\prime]\big(\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{X}_i\mathbf{X}_i^\prime]\big)^{-1}\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{X}_i Y_i] \\
  &= \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{X}_i Y_i] - \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{X}_i Y_i] = \mathbf{0}
  \end{aligned}
  $$

  $$\text{First entry of } \mathbf{X}_i \text{ is } 1 \;\Rightarrow\; \mathbb{E}[e_i] = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \Cov(X_{ij}, e_i) = \mathbb{E}[X_{ij}\, e_i] - \mathbb{E}[X_{ij}]\,\mathbb{E}[e_i] = 0$$

- This holds **mechanically** with respect to the BLP - no assumptions beyond the regularity conditions above!

:::

## Ordinary Least Squares

::: {.incremental}

- We have defined the **population** best linear predictor from a **minimization** problem

  $$m(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}^\prime \boldsymbol{\beta} \qquad \boldsymbol{\beta} = \arg\min_{\mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^k} \ \mathbb{E}\big[(Y_i - \mathbf{X}_i^\prime\mathbf{b})^2\big]$$

- And we've written $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ as a function of population expectations, $\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{X}_i\mathbf{X}_i^\prime]$ and $\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{X}_iY_i]$

  $$\boldsymbol{\beta} = \big(\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{X}_i\mathbf{X}_i^\prime]\big)^{-1}\,\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{X}_i Y_i]$$

- How do we estimate $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ from an i.i.d. **sample** from the target population?
- **Plug-in principle again**: replace each population expectation with a **sample mean**

  $$\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = \left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \mathbf{X}_i\mathbf{X}_i^\prime\right)^{-1} \left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \mathbf{X}_iY_i\right)$$

:::

## Why "least squares"?

::: {.incremental}

- We get the same estimator by applying the plug-in principle to the **minimization problem**
  - Minimize the **sample** mean of the squared errors

  $$\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = \arg\min_{\mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^k} \ \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - \mathbf{X}_i^\prime\mathbf{b})^2$$

- **Ordinary least squares** (OLS): the coefficients with the smallest **sum of squared residuals** (SSR)

- The same derivative as before but with a sample mean in place of the expectation gives the **normal equations**

  $$\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \mathbf{X}_i (Y_i - \mathbf{X}_i^\prime\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}) = \mathbf{0}$$

- So the **residuals** $\hat{e}_i = Y_i - \mathbf{X}_i^\prime\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ have the sample version of the projection error property
  - They average to $0$ and are uncorrelated with every covariate **in the sample**, by construction

:::

## OLS in matrix form

::: {.incremental}

- We'll typically talk about the **data** in terms of an $n$-length outcome vector and an $n \times k$ matrix of regressors 
  - One **row** per respondent and one **column** per variable.

  $$\underbrace{\mathbf{Y}}_{n \times 1} = \begin{pmatrix} Y_1 \\ Y_2 \\ \vdots \\ Y_n \end{pmatrix} \qquad \underbrace{\mathbf{X}}_{n \times k} = \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{X}_1^\prime \\ \mathbf{X}_2^\prime \\ \vdots \\ \mathbf{X}_n^\prime \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & X_{11} & \cdots & X_{1,k-1} \\ 1 & X_{21} & \cdots & X_{2,k-1} \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ 1 & X_{n1} & \cdots & X_{n,k-1} \end{pmatrix}$$

- The sums in $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ are **matrix products**

  $$\sum_{i=1}^n \mathbf{X}_i\mathbf{X}_i^\prime = \mathbf{X}^\prime\mathbf{X} \qquad \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbf{X}_iY_i = \mathbf{X}^\prime\mathbf{Y}$$

- The $\frac{1}{n}$'s cancel, which gives the common formula for OLS that you will often see:

  $$\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = (\mathbf{X}^\prime\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\prime\mathbf{Y}$$

:::

## Review: matrix multiplication

::: {.incremental}

- A $p \times n$ matrix times an $n \times q$ matrix is $p \times q$. 
  - Entry $(j, l)$ is the **inner product** of row $j$ of the first and column $l$ of the second

- Column $i$ of $\mathbf{X}^\prime$ is $\mathbf{X}_i$ and row $i$ of $\mathbf{X}$ is $\mathbf{X}_i^\prime$, so $\mathbf{X}^\prime\mathbf{X}$ is a **sum of outer products**

  $$\underbrace{\mathbf{X}^\prime}_{k \times n} \quad \underbrace{\mathbf{X}}_{n \times k} = \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{X}_1 & \mathbf{X}_2 & \cdots & \mathbf{X}_n \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{X}_1^\prime \\ \mathbf{X}_2^\prime \\ \vdots \\ \mathbf{X}_n^\prime \end{pmatrix} = \mathbf{X}_1\mathbf{X}_1^\prime + \mathbf{X}_2\mathbf{X}_2^\prime + \dotsc + \mathbf{X}_n\mathbf{X}_n^\prime$$

- Written out, $\mathbf{X}^\prime\mathbf{X}$ holds the **sums of squares and cross-products** of the columns of $\mathbf{X}$

  $$\mathbf{X}^\prime\mathbf{X} = \begin{pmatrix} n & \sum_i X_{i1} & \cdots & \sum_i X_{i,k-1} \\ \sum_i X_{i1} & \sum_i X_{i1}^2 & \cdots & \sum_i X_{i1}X_{i,k-1} \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \sum_i X_{i,k-1} & \sum_i X_{i,k-1}X_{i1} & \cdots & \sum_i X_{i,k-1}^2 \end{pmatrix} \qquad \mathbf{X}^\prime\mathbf{Y} = \begin{pmatrix} \sum_i Y_i \\ \sum_i X_{i1}Y_i \\ \vdots \\ \sum_i X_{i,k-1}Y_i \end{pmatrix}$$

:::

## When does the OLS estimator exist?

::: {.incremental}

- For the BLP, we assumed $\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{X}_i\mathbf{X}_i^\prime]$ is **invertible**
  - The sample version of this is that $\mathbf{X}^\prime\mathbf{X}$ must be invertible

- $\mathbf{X}^\prime\mathbf{X}$ is invertible if and only if $\mathbf{X}$ has **full column rank**

  $$\text{rank}(\mathbf{X}) = k$$

  - No column of $\mathbf{X}$ is a **linear combination** of the others
    - We have no **perfect** collinearity
  - And we need at least as many observations as coefficients, $n \geq k$

- Without full rank there is no **unique** $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ since there are **multiple** solutions which achieve the same minimum sum of squares.

:::

## Review: linear combinations and rank

::: {.incremental}

- A **linear combination** of the vectors $\mathbf{a}_1, \dotsc, \mathbf{a}_k$ is a weighted sum. A matrix times a vector is a linear combination of the matrix's **columns**

  $$\mathbf{A}\mathbf{c} = c_1\mathbf{a}_1 + c_2\mathbf{a}_2 + \dotsc + c_k\mathbf{a}_k$$

- The columns are **linearly independent** if the only combination equal to $\mathbf{0}$ is the trivial one: $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{0} \implies \mathbf{c} = \mathbf{0}$

- The **rank** of a matrix is the largest number of linearly independent columns it contains

  $$\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 5 & 6 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} \qquad \mathbf{a}_1 + \mathbf{a}_2 - \mathbf{a}_3 = \mathbf{0} \qquad \text{rank}(\mathbf{A}) = 2 < 3$$

:::

## Example: dummy variables

::: {.incremental}

- Consider three party categories: **Democrat**, **Independent** and **Republican** 
  - Code each category as a **dummy** (indicator) variable, e.g. $Z_i^{\text{Rep}} = I(\text{party}_i = \text{Republican})$

- What if we include an intercept **and** all three dummies?

  $$\begin{array}{l|cccc} & 1 & Z^{\text{Dem}} & Z^{\text{Ind}} & Z^{\text{Rep}} \\ \hline \text{Democrat} & 1 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ \text{Republican} & 1 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ \text{Independent} & 1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ \text{Democrat} & 1 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots \end{array}$$

  - Everyone is in exactly one category, so $Z^{\text{Dem}} + Z^{\text{Ind}} + Z^{\text{Rep}} = 1$: the intercept column. The rank is $3 < 4$

- If I include an intercept and **all** of these indicators, the OLS solution is undefined.
  - The fix is to drop one category which is the **baseline**
  - Each remaining dummy's coefficient compares its category to the baseline

:::

## Dummy variables in R

```{r}
anes <- anes |>
  mutate(party = case_when(pid7 <= 3 ~ "Democrat", pid7 == 4 ~ "Independent",
                           pid7 >= 5 ~ "Republican"),
         dem = as.numeric(party == "Democrat"),
         ind = as.numeric(party == "Independent"),
         rep = as.numeric(party == "Republican"))

# An intercept and all three dummies: R chooses a redundant column and drops it.
round(coef(lm(ft_trump ~ hostile_sexism + dem + ind + rep, data = anes)), 2)

# With factor variables, R automatically drops the first - by default the sort is alphabetical
round(coef(lm(ft_trump ~ hostile_sexism + party, data = anes)), 2)
```

## OLS with a single predictor

```{r}
#| label: ols-fits
#| include: false

# The fits used in the figures and text from here on
fit_hs <- lm(ft_trump ~ hostile_sexism, data = anes)
fit_party <- lm(ft_trump ~ hostile_sexism + party, data = anes)
fit_rr <- lm(ft_trump ~ hostile_sexism + racial_resentment, data = anes)
f1 <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f", x)
```


- With one covariate, $\mathbf{X}_i = (1, X_i)^\prime$ and $k = 2$. 
  - Solving $\mathbf{X}^\prime\mathbf{X}\,\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = \mathbf{X}^\prime\mathbf{Y}$ gives the plug-in version of the BLP we found before

  $$\hat{\beta}_1 = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar{X})(Y_i - \bar{Y})}{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar{X})^2} = \frac{\widehat{\Cov}(X_i, Y_i)}{\widehat{\Var}(X_i)} \qquad \hat{\beta}_0 = \bar{Y} - \hat{\beta}_1\bar{X}$$

## OLS with a single predictor

- In R, `lm()` fits OLS
  - Be careful with SEs here - they make the **classical** OLS assumptions - we'll talk about these next week

```{r}
summary(lm(ft_trump ~ hostile_sexism, data = anes))
```

## OLS with a single predictor

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 5.6
#| fig-align: center

# The OLS line over the scatterplot, labeled with its equation
b_hs <- coef(fit_hs)
base_plot() +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 0, xend = 1, y = b_hs[1], yend = b_hs[1] + b_hs[2]),
               colour = "#c5050c", linewidth = 1.6) +
  # The numbers go in as strings so plotmath keeps their trailing zeros
  annotate("text", x = 0.03, y = 96, hjust = 0, size = 7, colour = "#c5050c", parse = TRUE,
           label = sprintf("hat(Y) == '%.1f' + '%.1f' * X", b_hs[1], b_hs[2])) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 100))
```

::: {.incremental}

- $\hat{\beta}_1 = `r f1(b_hs[2])`$: respondents a quarter-point apart on the scale differ by `r f1(b_hs[2] / 4)` points on the thermometer, on average
- $\hat{\beta}_0 = `r f1(b_hs[1])`$: the predicted thermometer rating at the **lowest** level of hostile sexism

:::

## Adding partisanship

::: {.incremental}

- Partisanship predicts **both** hostile sexism and feelings about Trump. 
  - Add the party dummies, with Democrats as the baseline

  $$\hat{Y}_i = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 X_i + \hat{\beta}_2 Z_i^{\text{Ind}} + \hat{\beta}_3 Z_i^{\text{Rep}}$$

- Within each party, the fit is a **line** in $X_i$. The lines share a **slope** and have different **intercepts**

  $$\begin{aligned} \text{Democrats:} \quad & \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 X_i \\ \text{Independents:} \quad & (\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_2) + \hat{\beta}_1 X_i \\ \text{Republicans:} \quad & (\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_3) + \hat{\beta}_1 X_i \end{aligned}$$

- $\hat{\beta}_2$ and $\hat{\beta}_3$ are the **gaps** between the parallel lines: 
  - How much warmer Independents and Republicans are towards Trump than Democrats **with the same** level of hostile sexism
  - Assuming a **common slope** on hostile sexism across the three types of partisans.

:::

## Adding partisanship

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 5.6
#| fig-align: center

# The parallel lines of the party-dummy fit over the scatterplot, with each
# party's respondents in its color. Respondents in all three parties share
# the 17 values of X, so each party's points are nudged sideways a little to
# keep them from hiding one another
party_cols <- c(Democrat = "#0479a8", Independent = "#b8860b", Republican = "#c5050c")
b_p <- coef(fit_party)
party_lines <- tibble(party = names(party_cols),
                      a = b_p[1] + c(0, b_p["partyIndependent"], b_p["partyRepublican"]),
                      b = b_p["hostile_sexism"])
party_pts <- anes |>
  filter(!is.na(party)) |>
  mutate(x = hostile_sexism + c(Democrat = -0.014, Independent = 0, Republican = 0.014)[party])
ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = party_pts, aes(x, ft_trump, colour = party), alpha = 0.06, size = 3,
             stroke = 0) +
  geom_segment(data = party_lines, aes(x = 0, xend = 1, y = a, yend = a + b, colour = party),
               linewidth = 1.6) +
  geom_text(data = party_lines, aes(1.03, a + b, label = party, colour = party),
            hjust = 0, size = 6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = party_cols, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.25)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 100, 25)) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 1.2), ylim = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(x = "Hostile sexism", y = "Trump thermometer") +
  theme_reg
```

::: {.incremental}

- The slope falls from `r f1(b_hs[2])` to `r f1(b_p["hostile_sexism"])`. After accounting for the explanatory power of partisanship, the relationship is smaller but **still there**

:::

## Interacting with partisanship

::: {.incremental}

- To let the **slope** on hostile sexism differ between parties too we add **interactions**
  - The products of $X_i$ with each dummy

  $$\hat{Y}_i = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 X_i + \hat{\beta}_2 Z_i^{\text{Ind}} + \hat{\beta}_3 Z_i^{\text{Rep}} + \hat{\beta}_4 X_i Z_i^{\text{Ind}} + \hat{\beta}_5 X_i Z_i^{\text{Rep}}$$

- Within each party, the fit is still a line in $X_i$, but now each has its own intercept **and** slope

  $$\begin{aligned} \text{Democrats:} \quad & \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 X_i \\ \text{Independents:} \quad & (\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_2) + (\hat{\beta}_1 + \hat{\beta}_4) X_i \\ \text{Republicans:} \quad & (\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_3) + (\hat{\beta}_1 + \hat{\beta}_5) X_i \end{aligned}$$

- $\hat{\beta}_1$ is now the slope among **Democrats** (the baseline), and $\hat{\beta}_4$, $\hat{\beta}_5$ are **differences in slopes** relative to Democrats
- With every interaction in, this is the **same** as fitting a separate OLS line within each party

:::

## Interacting with partisanship

```{r}
#| label: fit-party-int
#| include: false
fit_pint <- lm(ft_trump ~ hostile_sexism * party, data = anes)
b_pi <- coef(fit_pint)
# Each party's slope: the baseline slope plus its difference
slope_p <- b_pi["hostile_sexism"] +
  c(0, b_pi["hostile_sexism:partyIndependent"], b_pi["hostile_sexism:partyRepublican"])
```

```{r}
# x * z in a formula adds x, z, and their product x:z
round(coef(lm(ft_trump ~ hostile_sexism * party, data = anes)), 2)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 3.9
#| fig-align: center

# The party lines again, now each with its own slope
party_int_lines <- tibble(party = names(party_cols),
                          a = b_pi[1] + c(0, b_pi["partyIndependent"], b_pi["partyRepublican"]),
                          b = slope_p)
ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = party_pts, aes(x, ft_trump, colour = party), alpha = 0.06, size = 3,
             stroke = 0) +
  geom_segment(data = party_int_lines, aes(x = 0, xend = 1, y = a, yend = a + b, colour = party),
               linewidth = 1.6) +
  geom_text(data = party_int_lines,
            aes(1.03, a + b, label = sprintf("%s (slope %.1f)", party, b), colour = party),
            hjust = 0, size = 5.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = party_cols, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.25)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 100, 25)) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 1.35), ylim = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(x = "Hostile sexism", y = "Trump thermometer") +
  theme_reg
```

- Slopes actually aren't that different!

## Interacting with education

::: {.incremental}

- Does the slope on hostile sexism differ by **education**? 
  - Let $Z_i^{\text{Col}} = I(\text{college degree}_i)$ and add its product with $X_i$

  $$\hat{Y}_i = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 X_i + \hat{\beta}_2 Z_i^{\text{Col}} + \hat{\beta}_3 X_i Z_i^{\text{Col}}$$

- Within each education group, the fit is a line in $X_i$ with its own intercept **and** slope

  $$\begin{aligned} \text{No college degree:} \quad & \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 X_i \\ \text{College degree:} \quad & (\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_2) + (\hat{\beta}_1 + \hat{\beta}_3) X_i \end{aligned}$$

- $\hat{\beta}_1$ is the slope among respondents **without** a degree (the baseline), and $\hat{\beta}_3$ is the **difference in slopes** for college graduates

:::

## Interacting with education

```{r}
#| label: fit-col-int
#| include: false
fit_cint <- lm(ft_trump ~ hostile_sexism * college, data = anes)
b_ci <- coef(fit_cint)
```

```{r}
round(coef(lm(ft_trump ~ hostile_sexism * college, data = anes)), 2)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| fig-align: center

# The two education groups' lines over the scatterplot, each group's
# respondents in its color and nudged sideways as in the party figures
col_cols <- c("No college degree" = "#b8860b", "College degree" = "#0479a8")
col_lines <- tibble(group = names(col_cols),
                    a = b_ci[1] + c(0, b_ci["college"]),
                    b = b_ci["hostile_sexism"] + c(0, b_ci["hostile_sexism:college"]))
col_pts <- anes |>
  filter(!is.na(college)) |>
  mutate(group = names(col_cols)[college + 1],
         x = hostile_sexism + if_else(college == 1, 0.008, -0.008))
ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = col_pts, aes(x, ft_trump, colour = group), alpha = 0.06, size = 3,
             stroke = 0) +
  geom_segment(data = col_lines, aes(x = 0, xend = 1, y = a, yend = a + b, colour = group),
               linewidth = 1.6) +
  geom_text(data = col_lines,
            aes(1.03, a + b, label = sprintf("%s (slope %.1f)", group, b), colour = group),
            hjust = 0, vjust = c(1.2, -0.2), size = 5.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = col_cols, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.25)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 100, 25)) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 1.45), ylim = c(0, 105)) +
  labs(x = "Hostile sexism", y = "Trump thermometer") +
  theme_reg
```

## A second continuous covariate

::: {.incremental}

- **Racial resentment**: a three question measure from @kinder1996divided, also averaged and re-scaled to $[0, 1]$ 
  - Correlated with hostile sexism: $r = `r sprintf("%.2f", cor(anes$hostile_sexism, anes$racial_resentment, use = "complete.obs"))`$

- With two continuous covariates, the fit is a **plane** over $(X_{i1}, X_{i2})$

  $$\hat{Y}_i = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 X_{i1} + \hat{\beta}_2 X_{i2}$$

:::

```{r}
round(coef(lm(ft_trump ~ hostile_sexism + racial_resentment, data = anes)), 2)
```

::: {.incremental}

- After partialling **racial resentment** out of both the outcome and hostile sexism, the slope on hostile sexism is `r f1(coef(fit_rr)[2])`, also down from the unconditional `r f1(b_hs[2])`

:::

## In three dimensions {.plane-slide}

```{r}
#| echo: false

# The two-covariate OLS fit as a surface through the 3D scatterplot. The
# animation (plane-anim/plane.js) turns the camera slowly while the slide is
# up; its fragments fade in a surface and bend it from the coefficients
# `from` into `beta` (each b0 + b1 x + b2 y + b3 xy), then draw the lines
# along it where racial resentment is held fixed
rr_pts <- anes |> filter(!is.na(racial_resentment))
b_rr <- coef(fit_rr)

plane_axis <- function(title, ...) {
  list(title = list(text = title, font = list(size = 15)), gridcolor = "#d9d9d9",
       zeroline = FALSE, showspikes = FALSE, showbackground = TRUE,
       backgroundcolor = "#EFEFEF", tickfont = list(size = 12), tickangle = 0, ...)
}

plane_widget <- function(beta, from, titles) {
  beta <- unname(c(beta, 0)[1:4])    # no interaction: b3 = 0
  from <- unname(c(from, 0)[1:4])
  surf <- function(h, r) beta[1] + beta[2] * h + beta[3] * r + beta[4] * h * r
  # A fine grid, since with an interaction the surface is curved
  pg <- seq(0, 1, 0.05)
  plane_z <- outer(pg, pg, \(r, h) surf(h, r))   # rows are y
  slice_rr <- c(0, 0.5, 1)
  slices <- list(x = unlist(lapply(slice_rr, \(r) c(0, 1, NA))),
                 y = unlist(lapply(slice_rr, \(r) c(r, r, NA))),
                 z = unlist(lapply(slice_rr, \(r) c(surf(0, r), surf(1, r), NA))))

  # Trace order matters: plane.js addresses traces by index
  p <- plotly::plot_ly(width = 1000, height = 560) |>
    plotly::add_trace(type = "scatter3d", mode = "markers", x = rr_pts$hostile_sexism,
                      y = rr_pts$racial_resentment, z = rr_pts$ft_trump, opacity = 0.12,
                      marker = list(size = 3, color = "#333333", line = list(width = 0)),
                      hoverinfo = "skip") |>
    plotly::add_surface(x = pg, y = pg, z = plane_z, opacity = 0.35, showscale = FALSE,
                        colorscale = list(c(0, "#0479a8"), c(1, "#0479a8")),
                        lighting = list(ambient = 1, diffuse = 0, specular = 0, fresnel = 0),
                        hoverinfo = "skip", visible = FALSE) |>
    plotly::add_trace(type = "scatter3d", mode = "lines", x = slices$x, y = slices$y,
                      z = slices$z, line = list(color = "#c5050c", width = 7),
                      connectgaps = FALSE, hoverinfo = "skip", visible = FALSE) |>
    plotly::layout(
      showlegend = FALSE,
      paper_bgcolor = "#F7F7F7",
      margin = list(l = 0, r = 0, t = 0, b = 0),
      font = list(family = "Red Hat Text, sans-serif", color = "#333333"),
      scene = list(
        xaxis = plane_axis("Hostile sexism", range = c(0, 1), tickvals = c(0, 0.5, 1)),
        yaxis = plane_axis("Racial resentment", range = c(0, 1), tickvals = c(0, 0.5, 1)),
        zaxis = plane_axis("Trump thermometer", range = c(-12, 105),
                           tickvals = seq(0, 100, 25)),
        aspectmode = "manual", aspectratio = list(x = 1.6, y = 1.6, z = 1.15),
        camera = list(projection = list(type = "orthographic")),   # set by the animation
        dragmode = "turntable", hovermode = FALSE
      )
    ) |>
    plotly::config(displayModeBar = FALSE, doubleClick = FALSE)

  p <- htmlwidgets::onRender(
    p,
    paste(readLines("plane-anim/plane.js"), collapse = "\n"),
    data = list(grid = pg, beta = beta, from = from, titles = titles)
  )

  # One empty fragment per animation step after the first
  htmltools::tagList(
    p,
    lapply(seq_len(length(titles) - 1), function(i) htmltools::span(class = "fragment pl-step"))
  )
}

# The plane rises from flat, at the mean of Y
plane_widget(b_rr, from = mean(rr_pts$ft_trump),
             titles = c("", "The regression plane", "Holding racial resentment fixed"))
```
